Serving Maine Since 1948

Testimony in Support of "An Act to Increase the Funding to the Live Fire Service Training Facilities Fund" LD 679
Presented to the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety Date: March 3, 2025 By: James A. Graves, Director, Maine Fire Service Institute
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Committee:
My name is James A. Graves, and I have the honor of serving as the Director of the Maine Fire Service Institute (MFSI). I am here today on behalf of the Maine Fire Services Institute, not on behalf of the Maine Community College System. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in strong support of this critical legislation, "An Act to Increase the Funding to the Live Fire Service Training Facilities Fund."
Firefighters in Maine face increasingly complex and dangerous environments. From structure fires to hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues, and wildland firefighting, their ability to respond effectively depends on high quality, hands-on training in controlled live fire conditions. Unfortunately, our regional live fire training facilities --essential to firefighter safety and proficiency-- are aging, deteriorating, and, in some cases, are no longer meeting the rigorous training demands of today's fire service.
This bill seeks a one-time allocation of $1,000,000 for fiscal year 2026-27 to support the construction, repair, and replacement of these essential training facilities across Maine. These funds, awarded through the Maine Fire Protection Services Commission, and administered through the Southern Maine Community College/Maine Fire Service Institute will ensure that firefighters across the state have access to safe, modern, and properly maintained live fire training environments.
The Urgent Need for Investment
1. Ensuring Firefighter Safety and Readiness: o Live fire training facilities allow firefighters to gain critical experience in real-world conditions, sharpening their skills before they face life-threatening emergencies in the field. o Without functioning training sites, many departments--especially in rural areas--struggle to provide their firefighters with the live fire experience necessary to meet the National Fire Protection Association fire training standards that MFSI has adopted to train and certify firefighters in Maine.
2. Addressing Facility Deterioration: o Many existing live fire-training facilities across Maine are outdated, with structural issues that limit their usability. o Some departments must travel long distances to access suitable training sites, increasing costs and reducing opportunities for regular live burn exercises.

4. Enhancing Public Safety: o Well-trained firefighters are better equipped to protect their communities, reducing property loss and improving life-saving outcomes. o By ensuring training sites are accessible and up to standard, Maine can continue to meet evolving fire service challenges effectively.
A Worthwhile Investment for Maine
The funding proposed in this bill is not just an expenditure--it is an investment in the safety of our firefighters and the communities they serve. Firefighters put their lives on the line daily, and they deserve the best possible training resources to do their jobs safely and effectively.
I urge this committee to support this bill and provide the funding needed to modernize and maintain Maine's regional live fire training facilities. By doing so, we reinforce our commitment to firefighter safety, strengthen the fire service statewide, and enhance the protection of Maine's residents and businesses. 10035318:
Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
In Support For
LD 679 - An Act to Increase the Funding to the Live Fire Service Training Facilities Fund
March 3, 2025
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee, my name is Rebecca Graham, and I am testifying in support for LD 679, at the direction of MMA's Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). Our LPC is made up of individuals from across Maine with municipal officials elected by their peers across Maine's 35 Senate districts representing communities with very different access to available enforcement resources and local capacity.
This fall, the Maine Municipal Association (MMA) held regional conversations with municipal officials and candidates from across the state. While the specific needs of each region varied, one common theme emerged everywhere: the urgent need for consistent and increased funding to support public safety, particularly through training. The current approach to training, however, is creating significant challenges. It undermines efforts to recruit new personnel to serve their communities and worsens disparities in resources, leaving rural Maine further behind when it comes to shared facilities.
A recurring concern voiced during these conversations was the difficulty of traveling long distances for training, the scheduling of training sessions at inconvenient times for volunteer staff, and the limited training options available.
LD 679 presents an opportunity for the state to strengthen its partnership with public safety agencies by investing in live fire training facilities. These facilities would improve shared resources across communities while being built to standards that protect both firefighters and the environment. By mitigating the harmful byproducts often encountered in live fire training, they would also allow responders to experience real-life stressors in a safe, controlled setting.
With recent environmental rule changes to the acceptable levels of ground contamination of polyfluoroalkyl, substances known commonly as PFAS and PFOA, live fire training through the historic method creates toxic waste that potentially contaminates ground water and soils. While this substance is ubiquitous and prevalent in many of the items we use on a daily basis, elimination from water and ground sources is an enormous challenge and costing governments and individuals thousands of dollars.
Live fire training sites are extremely important, not only in preparing municipal fire volunteers for the realities of a structure fire, but also for environmental protection, and the safety of fire fighters.

Currently, the community college system relies on training facilities funded and maintained by other localities. It's essential for the state to take a more active role in supporting and maintaining these facilities, ensuring a more effective partnership in public safety. LD 679 may be a small step, but it's an important one that signals the state's commitment to supporting the safety of both residents and visitors. As Maine continues to benefit from tourism, the burden of funding public safety largely falls on local residents who serve in these vital roles.
For these reasons, we urge you to consider investing General Fund revenue in public safety, and specifically in LD 679.

LD 679 - An Act to Increase the Funding to the Live Fire Service Training Facilities Fund
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and honorable members of the Criminal Justice and
Public Safety Committee, my name is Shawn Esler, and it is a privilege to serve as the State Fire Marshal.
I write neither for nor against LD 679.
In 2023, the fire service across Maine responded to 178,463 calls for service. Those callouts included structure fires, explosions, technical rescues, hazardous materials events, emergency medical calls, and other hazardous situations. Every day, our first responders put themselves in harm's way to ensure the safety of the residents and visitors of our great State.
Maine is one of the few States that does not have a statewide fire academy, and we do not own any fire
training facilities. Maine relies on the Maine Fire Service Institute (MFSI), a department of Southern
Maine Community College to deliver fire training across the State. Funding for both MFSI and the Office
of State Fire Marshal is appropriated through the fire insurance premium tax outlined in Title 25 section
2399. This firnding does not cover the cost to fully support either organization, therefore we do not have
the funds available to support repairing or building facilities.
While a centrally located statewide fire academy would be ideal, the initial cost would be high, and it would require annual support through the State budget. Additionally, meeting the needs of rural volunteer fire departments spread all over our State poses a challenge. In 2018, the Maine Fire Protection Services Commission conducted a gap analysis to determine the training needs of Maine's fire service.
Eleven (l 1) live fire training facilities and potential building sites were identified across the State that are
within an hour's drive of most fire departments. A comprehensive and fiscally responsible plan was
created, so that over time, these smaller cost-effective facilities could be repaired and built out to support firefighter training. Today, the State has funded the replacement of one facility in Yarmouth, the repairs
of a facility in Auburn, and has constructed two facilities in Farmington and Farfield. More work needs to be done to repair and construct these facilities in northern, eastern, and downeast Maine to achieve that
goal.
It's important that our firefighters have access to live fire training facilities for several reasons that include enhancing public safety, increasing firefighter safety and operational readiness, reducing liability for our communities, supporting recruitment and retention efforts, and equally as important, readying the next generation of first responders. Across our State, our firefighters stand ready to answer the call for help and training facilities greatly support that mission.

Testimony of Vicki Schmidt, Hebron ME in support of LD 679, An Act to Increase the Funding to the Live Fire Service Training Facilities Fund
March 3rd, 2025 Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Committee On Criminal Justice & Public Safety
Thank you for today's opportunity, I am Vicki Schmidt from Hebron Maine and I serve with the Buckfield Fire Department, a 14-member volunteer department in Western Maine. I also represent Volunteer & On-call Firefighters on the Maine Fire Protection Services Commission.
As a volunteer firefighter and a State Fire Instructor III with the Maine Fire Services Institute for over twenty years. I urge your support and funding of LD679. My experience has given me a very good understanding of what it takes to train, and as importantly maintain, a firefighter at skilled performance standards.
In the seven years since 2018, and the fully unanimous passing and initial funding support of LD 1845 by the 128th Maine Legislature, Maine's fire community has worked diligently to reverse the lack of National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) compliant fire training infrastructure for Maine.
The collaborative efforts of Maine firefighters, our professional associations, our instructors, town officials, Maine Fire Services Institute and the Southern Maine Community College have been nothing short of commendable. Every penny of the funding and grant awards is, or is in the process of, being completely used for the repair, replacement, or construction of NFPA compliant Live Fire Training Facilities. Furthermore, the grant design ensures the commitment, integrity, and responsibility for the future longevity of these regional facilities.
The Fire Commission has successfully led this charge and many Commission members have volunteered hundreds of hours to help establish these improvements. The value of the state funding and its return on investment to provide the basis for these facilities can not be under estimated. The funding is significantly leveraged by local towns who secure donations, volunteer time and provide hours of work and services to further amplify the grant funding. This is a fully win-win situation for taxpayers, our town and department, the firefighters of Maine, and most importantly, the citizens and property we are dedicated to protect.
Our State goal for these facilities also provides many inherent values that are not easy to ascertain. One of the most important is the consistency of their design and operation making them more predictable and efficient to teach and instruct with. Instructors and program managers can better plan and manage all types of training in these facilities; particularly live fire training, which is some of the most challenging to teach, especially with new recruits.

LD679 Schmidt pg 2 of 2
The Fire Commissions goal to have a Live Fire Training Facility within an hour's travel time for 90% of Maine firefighters is not only a noble goal, it is a necessary one. It reduces costs for municipalities while ensuring efficient access to certified training. Not only has certified training proven to be one of the most important retention strategies for trained firefighters, it further works to reduce firefighter death, injuries, and workers compensation insurance claims. (Report on Firefighter Training to the 1998 Legislature Minnesota) https://www.mbfte.org/Forms/WebsiteMenu/1998-022.pdf
As you are aware, firefighters want to serve and protect, and we are the last to ask for help. I urge your support and successful funding of LD679. I can guarantee the Fire Commission, along with the fire services of Maine, will continue to ensure our fire training facility program success.
Thank you,
Vicki Schmidt Firefighter, Buckfield ME Maine Fire Services Instructor III Maine State Federation of Firefighter, Volunteer & On-Call Firefighters 207-890-4590 troika@meglalink.net
